newsitem.title: USA: Union prepares to strike at United Parcel Service.
newsitem.headline: Union prepares to strike at United Parcel Service.

text.p: The International Brotherhood of Teamsters prepared on Sunday to go on strike against United Parcel Service, the biggest U.S. shipper, with contract talks at a standstill.

The Teamsters sent a revised contract proposal to the company on Saturday, but no negotiations were scheduled as of noon EDT (1600 GMT) Sunday. The union set a strike deadline of midnight EDT (0400 on Monday GMT).

"We're waiting to hear from the company. The ball's in their court," said Rand Wilson, a union spokesman. "They have to come to the table and negotiate. Otherwise at midnight tonight, there will be a strike."

Wilson said the Teamsters had made "slight modifications" in their latest offer based on the 15 hours of talks over two days with the company and federal mediators. He declined to discuss the substance of the changes.
UPS and officials of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service in Washington did not return repeated phone calls seeking comment.

More than 185,000 Teamster package sorters, loaders and drivers were scheduled to walk out in the absence of a new contract shifting more workers into full-time jobs than the company has agreed to so far.

About 60 percent of UPS workers are part-timers, according to the union, which wants the company to provide thousands of new full-time job openings. The company proposed on Wednesday night to create 200 new full-time jobs per year from part-time positions, the union said.
The union and UPS also remain apart on curbing the company's ability to subcontract jobs, strengthening pension benefits and boosting health and safety standards.
With its trademark brown trucks, UPS normally handles an estimated four-fifths of the packages shipped by ground nationwide.

But the threat of a strike has hurt business at UPS, which typically delivers 12 million packages a day. The company said last week it was losing about $5 million a day in business to competitors such as the U.S. Postal Service and Federal Express Corp.

Talks between the union and Atlanta-based UPS were recessed on Friday night. The union postponed an initial strike deadline of midnight Thursday at the request of federal mediation service director John Calhoun Wells.
On Saturday UPS expressed interest in continuing talks, but a company spokeswoman, Gina Ellrich, called it "very unfortunate" that a new deadline had been set.
With revenue of $22.4 billion in 1996, UPS annually handles about three billion parcels and documents, shipped to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centres.
